# Draft:Battle of Dujayl (1258)

The Battle of Dujayl was the first and last pitched battle between the Abbasid Caliphate and Baiju Noyan, the commander under Hulagu Khan (who was appointed as the governor-general of Syria and Egypt by Möngke Khan).
Background
Möngke Khan, elected as Great Khan in 1251, appointed his brother Hulagu as the governor-general of Syria and Egypt to further expand the borders of the Mongol Empire. Leading a massive army (approx. 120,000), Hulagu marched through Khorasan, Iran, and Iraq, consolidating Mongol rule in the region. He wiped the Order of Assassins (Hashshashins) in Mazandaran from the stage of history. Since his army fought in Muslim lands, he sent envoys to the Crusaders, Georgians, and Armenians, forming a Christian alliance with reinforcements.
Seeking to initially annex the Caliphate through diplomacy, Hulagu sent envoys to the Abbasid Caliph al-Musta'sim, offering vassalage. Under pressure from his vizier, Ibn al-Alqami, the Caliph rejected the offer, called for Jihad among Muslim rulers, and began preparations in Baghdad.
The Advance
On March 27, 1257, Hulagu launched his campaign toward Baghdad. To prevent reinforcements from reaching the city, he split his army into three columns. He ordered Kitbuqa to besiege Baghdad from the south, took command of the center himself, and left the right wing to Baiju Noyan. Baiju’s column marched through Erbil toward Mosul to besiege Baghdad from the west. With a bridge of boats built by the Atabeg of Mosul, Badr al-Din Lu'lu', Baiju crossed the Tigris and moved south to Tikrit, where he was reinforced by troops sent from Hamadan.
The Battle
To stop the Mongol forces approaching from the north, Caliph al-Musta'sim dispatched a force of 20,000 (consisting of Kurdish soldiers) under the command of Mujahid al-Din Aybak (Devatdar-i Saghir). The two armies met at Anbar, northwest of Baghdad.
An advance guard under Buka Timur engaged the Abbasid forces and performed a feigned retreat. Aybak, mistaking this for a Mongol defeat, ordered a pursuit. At Dujayl, the Mongols launched a fierce counter-attack from an ambush prepared by Baiju Noyan. As neither side gained a clear advantage by sunset, they camped for the night.
During the night, the Mongols destroyed the dykes of the Dujayl River, flooding the plains behind the Abbasid army. The next morning, the Mongols launched a sudden assault, routing the Caliph's forces. Most soldiers were killed in combat, and those who fled drowned in the floodwaters.
Aftermath
Mujahid al-Din Aybak managed to escape with a small force and reached Baghdad after facing several attacks along the way. Upon his return, he accelerated the fortification of the city walls, realizing the defensive measures were insufficient. With this victory, Mongol forces continued their advance, besieging the western walls of Baghdad and cutting off all relief routes.
